query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In laser‐cladded high-entropy alloy (HEA) protective coatings, the intentional co‐doping with small amounts of Y and Hf refines and stabilizes the microstructure—by inhibiting grain growth and promoting well‐distributed oxide or intermetallic precipitates—that in turn reduces the initiation and propagation of wear damage under high-temperature, high-load conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy coating (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1) processed by laser cladding without Y/Hf additions, displaying a mixed FCC+BCC microstructure with relatively larger grain sizes and less stabilized oxide/intermetallic features.
generation.intervention: Laser cladding of the same HEA composition but co-doped with small amounts of Y and Hf (YHf-EHEA), under otherwise identical processing parameters.
generation.conditions: Wear tests conducted at elevated temperatures (around 900 °C) and under conditions representative of high-temperature corrosive or abrasive environments (e.g., molten salt exposure or mechanical sliding load conditions).
generation.structural_mediator: Grain size refinement and stabilization of the microstructure via precipitate/oxide phase formation (e.g., enhanced formation of an Al-rich L12 or similar dispersoids) mediated by the segregation of Y and Hf at grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Y and Hf atoms preferentially segregate to grain boundaries and phase interfaces during laser cladding and subsequent heat exposure, which delays grain coarsening and promotes the formation of a more continuous and stable protective scale. This stable microstructure reduces the development of micro-cracks and the material removal during wear, thereby enhancing wear resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline HEA coating, the Y/Hf co-doped coating will exhibit lower wear rates, reduced surface micro-cracking, and improved overall wear performance over the test temperature range. Observations should include a statistically significant reduction in wear volume and a finer, more stable microstructure after exposure.
generation.baseline: HEA coatings prepared by laser cladding using the standard AlCoCrFeNi2.1 composition without Y and Hf co-doping.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for wear-resistant applications in high-temperature environments (approximately up to 900 °C) where thermal stability and microstructural integrity are challenging, but may not apply if the wear mechanism is dominated by factors unrelated to microstructure, such as extremely aggressive chemical attack.
generation.uncertainty: The exact nature (composition, size, distribution) of the precipitated phases or oxide scales formed due to Y/Hf addition and their quantitative contribution to wear reduction still require detailed microstructural and tribological analyses. Additionally, the interplay between these microstructural changes and various wear mechanisms (e.g., adhesive, abrasive, or fatigue wear) under different loading conditions is not fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy coatings via laser cladding: one set using baseline AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy and the other with identical composition co-doped with low concentrations of Y and Hf. Subject both sets to identical wear testing at high temperatures (around 900 °C) under controlled sliding or abrasive wear conditions. Use identical load and sliding speeds.
measurements: Quantitative wear rate (e.g., volume loss per unit distance)
Surface micro-crack density and wear scar morphology via SEM
Grain size and phase distribution characterization (e.g., via XRD, TEM, or SEM-EDX) before and after wear tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the co-doped Y/Hf coatings do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in wear rate and micro-crack density compared to the baseline coatings, or if microstructural analysis does not reveal evidence of grain refinement/precipitate stabilization attributable to Y/Hf additions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

The solidification microstructure, thermal stability, and hot corrosion performance of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts were investigated. The experimental results showed that the structure of the as-deposited coatings consisted of FCC and BCC/B2 phases. After heat treatment, an Al-rich L12 phase was precipitated in the FCC phase of all coatings. The grain sizes of the EHEA and YHf-EHEA coatings after heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h increased by 27.5% and 15.7%, respectively, compared to the as-deposited coatings. Meanwhile, after hot corrosion, the spallation areas of the YHf-EHEA and EHEA coatings accounted for 14.98% and 5.67% of the total surface area, respectively. Especially in high-temperature applications, the microstructure of EHEA, with FCC+BCC phases, exhibits characteristics that are similar to the γ′ phase of nickel-based alloys, which has demonstrated outstanding resistance to oxidation [,]. Moreover, the unique eutectic solidification structure of EHEA provides a lower phase interface energy, and the significant sluggish diffusion effects characteristic of high-entropy alloys show its superior stability at higher temperatures [,]. Therefore, EHEA has great potential as a high-temperature protective coating. On the other hand, exploration of the properties of alloying elements and rare earth elements for high-entropy alloys has also never stopped [,,,]. Research about the effect of alloying elements on the performance of HEAs has predominantly concentrated on the mechanical properties while the literature indicates that conventional and high-entropy alloys and Y and Hf co-doping can effectively enhance the high-temperature oxidation resistance of alloys [,,]. AlCoCrFeNi alloy is a typical type of HEA, and its oxidation resistance has been attracting much attention. It has been found that Al2O3 and Cr2O3 scales are formed on AlxCoCrFeNi alloys due to the selective oxidation of Al and Cr at high temperatures [,,,,]. Alloys can have greater oxidation resistance if the continuity and internal position of the Al2O3 scales are improved by enhancing the content of Al []. Lu concluded that the oxidation of AlCoCrFeNi alloys would be slower if small amounts of Y and Hf were added []. Their oxidation behavior was studied by Butler and Weaver in dry air at 1050 °C []. It has been suggested that they are the perfect material for high-temperature constructional praxis as they have strong oxidation resistance and structural stability. Therefore, AlCoCrFeNi alloys have been proposed as high performance antioxidant coating materials for protecting the high temperature components of aero-engines or as bonded coating materials in TBCs.
